rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording says ‘most’ rather than ‘all’ because God knew that some among them would believe.
rows.anchor: ولم يقل أنهم لأن منهم من قد علم أنه يؤمن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their hearing would mean listening receptively, or reflecting on the Prophet’s words and understanding them; in practice they are as if deaf and unreasoning.
rows.anchor: سماع قبول أو يفكرون فيما تقول فيعقلونه أي هم بمنزلة من لا يعقل ولا يسمع

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Because they gain no benefit from what they hear, it is as though they did not hear; the intended people are the Meccans.
rows.anchor: لما لم ينتفعوا بما يسمعون فكأنهم لم يسمعوا والمراد أهل مكة

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Here أَمْ has the sense of بل (rather).
rows.anchor: قيل: { أم } بمعنى بل في مثل هذا الموضع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They resemble cattle in eating and drinking, without reflecting on the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: أي في الأكل والشرب لا يفكرون في الآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They are further astray because cattle face neither reckoning nor punishment.
rows.anchor: إذ لا حساب ولا عقاب على الأنعام

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Animals recognize their Lord, find their pastures, and obey their handlers, while these people neither obey nor recognize their Creator and Provider.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل: البهائم تعرف ربها وتهتدي إلى مراعيها وتنقاد لأربابها

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Animals cannot reason out the truth of monotheism and prophethood, but they also do not believe those truths false.
rows.anchor: لأن البهائم إن لم تعقل صحة التوحيد والنبوة لم تعتقد بطلان ذلك أيضا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘The Most Merciful’ means God Most High.
rows.anchor: { وإذا قيل لهم اسجدوا للرحمن } أي لله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their question expresses denial and astonishment: they knew ‘the Merciful’ only as the false prophet Musaylima of Yamama.
rows.anchor: على جهة الإنكار والتعجب، أي ما نعرف الرحمن

rows.speaker: القاضي أبو بكر ابن العربي
rows.claim: He argues that they rejected the attribute, not the one described, because they asked ‘what is the Merciful?’ rather than ‘who is the Merciful?’
rows.anchor: وزعم القاضي أبو بكر ابن العربي أنهم إنما جهلوا الصفة لا الموصوف

rows.speaker: ابن الحصار
rows.claim: He objects that Ibn al-Arabi seems to have missed 13:30, which says that they disbelieved in the Merciful.
rows.anchor: قال ابن الحصار: وكأنه رحمه الله لم يقرأ الآية الأخرى وهم يكفرون بالرحمن

rows.speaker: المدنيون والبصريون
rows.claim: They read تأمرنا with تاء: ‘Shall we prostrate to what you, Muhammad, command us?’ Abu Ubayd and Abu Hatim prefer this reading.
rows.anchor: هذه قراءة المدنيين والبصريين أي لما تأمرنا أنت يا محمد

rows.speaker: الأعمش وحمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: They read يأمرنا with ياء, which Abu Ubayd interprets as referring to the Merciful; he says accepting the Merciful’s command would have prevented their disbelief.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الأعمش وحمزة والكسائي: { يأمرنا } بالياء

rows.speaker: أبو عبيد
rows.claim: He argues that if they acknowledged that the Merciful commanded them, they would not be disbelievers.
rows.anchor: قال: ولو أقروا بأن الرحمن أمرهم ما كانوا كفارا

rows.speaker: النحاس
rows.claim: For the ya-reading, he prefers ‘what the Prophet commands us’; this avoids imposing a strained interpretation, though he says the ta-reading is clearer and more direct.
rows.anchor: فقال النحاس: وليس يجب أن يتأول عن الكوفيين في قراءتهم هذا التأويل البعيد، ولكن الأولى أن يكون التأويل لهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Being told to prostrate to the Merciful increased their aversion to the religion.
rows.anchor: أي زادهم قول القائل لهم اسجدوا للرحمن نفورا عن الدين

rows.speaker: سفيان الثوري
rows.claim: He says devotionally that what increases God’s enemies in aversion increases his own submission to God.
rows.anchor: وكان سفيان الثوري يقول في هذه الآية: إلهي زادني لك خضوعا ما زاد عداك نفورا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After describing the idolaters’ ignorance and attacks on revelation and prophethood, the passage turns to believing servants and honors them by attributing them to God; this echoes 17:1.
rows.anchor: لما ذكر جهالات المشركين وطعنهم في القرآن والنبوة ذكر عباده المؤمنين أيضا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who obey God and devote their faculties to His commands deserve the name ‘servants’; the opposite are like cattle for failing to reflect, as discussed at 7:179.
rows.anchor: فمن أطاع الله وعبده وشغل سمعه وبصره ولسانه وقلبه بما أمره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sentence implies هم: ‘God’s servants are those who walk on earth’; the example is ‘Zayd [is] the prince.’
rows.anchor: وكأنه قال: وعباد الرحمن هم الذين يمشون على الأرض، فحذف هم

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: He takes الذين as the predicate of an omitted subject.
rows.anchor: ف { الذين } خبر مبتدأ محذوف قاله الأخفش

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: He says the predicate may be the closing promise ‘those will be rewarded with the upper chamber’; the intervening material describes them, though he also allows الذين يمشون as predicate.
rows.anchor: وما بين المبتدأ والخبر أوصاف لهم وما تعلق بها قاله الزجاج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Walking represents their whole life and conduct; movement on earth is a fitting choice because it entails living and mixing with people.
rows.anchor: و { يمشون } عبارة عن عيشهم ومدة حياتهم وتصرفاتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: هَوْنًا is the verbal noun of هَيِّن and denotes calmness and dignity.
rows.anchor: قوله تعالى: { هونا } الهون مصدر الهين وهو من السكينة والوقار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The tafsir describes them as forbearing, humble people who walk moderately; measured pace and good bearing are prophetic traits.
rows.anchor: وفي «التفسير»: يمشون على الأرض حلماء متواضعين

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A prophetic report urges people to keep calm, since righteousness is not in rushing.
rows.anchor: أيها الناس عليكم بالسكينة فإن البر ليس في الإيضاع

rows.speaker: القاضي عياض
rows.claim: The Prophet’s gait is described as firm and quick in lifting the feet, purposeful in its sway, broad-striding, and gentle rather than swaggering or hurried.
rows.anchor: ويخطو تكفؤا، ويمشي هونا، ذريع المشية إذا مشى كأنما ينحط من صبب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He glosses the gait terms: تكفؤ is a purposeful lean, هون is gentleness and dignity, and ذريع means broad-striding; the pace is steady without haste.
rows.anchor: التقلع، رفع الرجل بقوة والتكفؤ: الميل إلى سنن المشي وقصده

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: Umar used to walk quickly by natural disposition, not by affectation.
rows.anchor: وكان عمر بن الخطاب رضي الله عنه يسرع جبلة لا تكلفا

rows.speaker: الزهري
rows.claim: He says that fast walking removes the face’s dignity.
rows.anchor: قال الزهري: سرعة المشي تذهب بهاء الوجه

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: He understands the disapproved pace as strenuous haste, which compromises dignity; moderation is best.
rows.anchor: يريد الإسراع الحثيث لأنه يخل بالوقار والخير في التوسط

rows.speaker: زيد بن أسلم
rows.claim: After searching for the meaning, he reports a dream answer: they are people who do not intend to corrupt the earth.
rows.anchor: هم الذين لا يريدون أن يفسدوا في الأرض

rows.speaker: القشيري
rows.claim: They do not walk toward corruption and sin, but toward obedience and permissible affairs, without frivolous conduct.
rows.anchor: قال القشيري: وقيل لا يمشون لإفساد ومعصية، بل في طاعة الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse links to the prohibition on walking arrogantly in 31:18.
rows.anchor: ولا تمش في الأرض مرحا إن الله لا يحب كل مختال فخور

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: He explains their walk as obedience, good conduct, and humility.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: بالطاعة والمعروف والتواضع

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: They are forbearing: when ignorant people treat them ignorantly, they do not answer in kind.
rows.anchor: الحسن حلماء إن جهل عليهم لم يجهلوا

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another explanation is that they do not behave arrogantly toward people.
rows.anchor: وقيل: لا يتكبرون على الناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He treats these interpretations as close and gathers them under knowledge of God, fear of Him, and awareness of His judgments and punishment.
rows.anchor: قلت: وهذه كلها معان متقاربة، ويجمعها العلم بالله والخوف منه

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: One group attaches هَوْنًا directly to walking, taking the verse to describe a gentle gait alone.
rows.anchor: وذهبت فرقة إلى أن { هونا } مرتبط بقوله: { يمشون على الأرض }

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: He allows that their character should match their gait, but rejects gait alone as the meaning: even a sly wolf may walk slowly.
rows.anchor: ويشبه أن يتأول هذا على أن تكون أخلاق ذلك الماشي هونا مناسبة لمشيه

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: The Prophet himself walked with a purposeful sway, as if descending a slope, and was the foremost model for the community.
rows.anchor: وقد كان رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يتكفأ في مشيه كأنما ينحط في صبب

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The instruction to walk slowly when pursuing an aim concerns the resolve within oneself, not gait alone.
rows.anchor: من مشى منكم في طمع فليمش رويدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some hypocrites who feigned religious adherence copied only the outward slow gait; a satirical couplet says they all walk slowly while hunting prey.
rows.anchor: كلهم يمشي رويد كلهم يطلب صيد

rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: In his own verse he contrasts humility amid high rank with inner purity, observing that people’s quietness often comes from arrogance.
rows.anchor: تواضعت في العلياء والأصل كابر وحزت قصاب السبق بالهون في الأمر

rows.speaker: النحاس
rows.claim: He says سلاما is not a greeting of peace but a request for disengagement, meaning ‘I am clear of you’; grammatically it may be governed by قالوا or be a verbal noun, as Sibawayh holds.
rows.anchor: قال النحاس: ليس { سلاما } من التسليم إنما هو من التسلم

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: He allows سلاما to be an accusative verbal noun.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون مصدرا وهذا قول سيبويه

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: He says قالوا governs سلاما because the sense is that they said this expression.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: والذي أقوله: أن { قالوا } هو العامل

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: He interprets سلاما as sound or right speech: they gently deflect an ignorant person with words.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: معنى { سلاما } سدادا

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: Another group says the person addressed should utter the actual word سلاما, meaning ‘we depart in peace’; a verb from the same root governs it.
rows.anchor: وقالت فرقة: ينبغي للمخاطب أن يقول للجاهل سلاما بهذا اللفظ

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: Some say the Meccan verse was abrogated for unbelievers by the sword verse, while its etiquette remains for Muslims.
rows.anchor: هذه الآية كانت قبل آية السيف

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: He argues Muslims were not then commanded to greet polytheists; سلاما means seeking safety and neutrality, with neither good nor evil between the groups.
rows.anchor: قال سيبويه: لم يؤمر المسلمون يومئذ أن يسلموا على المشركين

rows.speaker: النحاس
rows.claim: He says he knows no other discussion of abrogation by Sibawayh besides this verse.
rows.anchor: ولا نعلم لسيبويه كلاما في معنى الناسخ والمنسوخ إلا في هذه الآية

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: He says the point should be phrased as Muslims not yet being commanded to fight them, and later being commanded to fight.
rows.anchor: المبرد: كان ينبغي أن يقال: لم يؤمر المسلمون يومئذ بحربهم ثم أمروا بحربهم

rows.speaker: محمد بن يزيد
rows.claim: He says Sibawayh was wrong and expressed himself badly.
rows.anchor: محمد بن يزيد: أخطأ سيبويه في هذا وأساء العبارة

rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: He says Muslims were neither ordered nor forbidden to greet polytheists then; they were ordered to pardon and graciously avoid them, and the Prophet visited their gatherings without compromising.
rows.anchor: ابن العربي: لم يؤمر المسلمون يومئذ أن يسلموا على المشركين ولا نهوا عن ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He finds Ibn al-Arabi’s position more consistent with the Sunnah and rejects the need to claim abrogation; he notes scholarly disagreement about greeting unbelievers in Surat Maryam.
rows.anchor: قلت: هذا القول أشبه بدلائل السنة

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: In al-Khalil’s anecdote, an Arab explains that Abu Rabi‘ah’s command استووا meant ‘go up’ to the roof.
rows.anchor: وقد ذكر النضر بن شميل قال حدثني الخليل قال: أتيت أبا ربيعة الأعرابي

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalil links the Arab’s explanation of استووا as ‘ascend’ to the wording about God turning to heaven in 41:11; later Abu Rabi‘ah’s سلاما means leaving matters at neither good nor harm, echoing this verse.
rows.anchor: قال الخليل: هو من قول الله عز وجل

rows.speaker: النضر بن شميل
rows.claim: He transmits al-Khalil’s account that Abu Rabi‘ah used سلاما to ask for a neutral parting, which the adjacent Arab glossed from this Qur’anic verse.
rows.anchor: قال فقال الأعرابي: إنه سألكم متاركة لا خير فيها ولا شر

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: A historical report says Ibrahim ibn al-Mahdi, who opposed Ali, dreamed of repeatedly challenging Ali’s claim to leadership; Ali answered سلاما, and the narrator says he may have forgotten the verse.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: ورأيت في بعض التواريخ أن إبراهيم بن المهدي

rows.speaker: المأمون
rows.claim: The Ma’mun identifies Ali’s سلاما as the most eloquent answer from this verse; Ibrahim is embarrassed, and the narrator says the dream was surely true.
rows.anchor: فنبه المأمون على الآية من حضره وقال: هو والله يا عم علي بن أبي طالب

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: He takes رسول to mean ‘message’, making the phrase ‘we are bearers of the message of the Lord of the worlds’; he cites poetry for this usage.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عبيدة: رسول بمعنى رسالة والتقدير على هذا إنا ذوو رسالة رب العالمين

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: He also says رسول can be a singular form for two or a group, as in Arabic ‘this is my messenger/agent’ for singular, dual, or plural; he cites 26:77.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عبيد: ويجوز أن يكون الرسول في معنى الاثنين والجمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Send the Children of Israel with us’ means release them and let them go with Moses and Aaron to Palestine instead of enslaving them.
rows.anchor: أي أطلقهم وخل سبيلهم حتى يسيروا معنا إلى فلسطين ولا تستعبدهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh had enslaved the Israelites for four hundred years; at that time they numbered 630,000.
rows.anchor: وكان فرعون استعبدهم أربعمائة سنة، وكانوا في ذلك الوقت ستمائة ألف وثلاثين ألفا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brothers were refused an audience for a year; Pharaoh then admitted them, expecting to laugh at a man claiming to be a messenger.
rows.anchor: فانطلقا إلى فرعون فلم يؤذن لهما سنة في الدخول عليه، فدخل البواب على فرعون

rows.speaker: وهب وغيره
rows.claim: They report that Pharaoh displayed lions, tigers, and leopards; the beasts rushed to Moses and Aaron, licked them, wagged their tails, and pressed their cheeks to their thighs, astonishing Pharaoh.
rows.anchor: وروى وهب وغيره: أنهما لما دخلا على فرعون وجداه وقد أخرج سباعا من أسد ونمور وفهود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh invokes Moses’ childhood upbringing to boast and belittle him: he raised him as a child and spared him when others were killed.
rows.anchor: على جهة المن عليه والاحتقار. أي ربيناك صغيرا ولم نقتلك من جملة من قتلنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: By asking how Moses spent years among them, Pharaoh challenges when Moses acquired the authority he now claims.
rows.anchor: فمتى كان هذا الذي تدعيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh then reproaches Moses for killing the Egyptian and asks how he can claim that God sent him while his past is known.
rows.anchor: ثم قرره بقتل القبطي بقوله: { وفعلت فعلتك التي فعلت }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fatḥa reading فعلتك is preferable because it denotes one occurrence; al-Sha‘bi’s kasra reading denotes a manner, state, or known habit.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الشعبي: { فعلتك } بكسر الفاء والفتح أولى لأنها المرة الواحدة

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: The poet’s simile for a woman’s gait illustrates the kasra reading’s sense of a manner or state.
rows.anchor: كأن مشيتها من بيت جارتها مر السحابة لا ريث ولا عجل

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: He takes ‘you were among the disbelievers’ to mean Moses was culpable in killing the Egyptian, whose life was unlawful to take.
rows.anchor: قال الضحاك: أي في قتلك القبطي إذ هو نفس لا يحل قتله

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: He interprets it as being ungrateful for Pharaoh’s favor of upbringing and care.
rows.anchor: أي بنعمتي التي كانت لنا عليك من التربية والإحسان إليك قاله ابن زيد

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: He says Pharaoh means that Moses disbelieved in Pharaoh’s claim to be his god.
rows.anchor: الحسن: { من الكافرين } في أني إلهك

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: He says Moses was counted among disbelievers in God because he had shared the Egyptians’ religion, which he now condemns.
rows.anchor: السدي: { من الكافرين } بالله لأنك كنت معنا على ديننا هذا الذي تعيبه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Eleven years and some months passed between Moses’ flight after killing the Egyptian and his return as a prophet.
rows.anchor: وكان بين خروج موسى عليه السلام حين قتل القبطي وبين رجوعه نبيا أحد عشر عاما غير أشهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses admits that he committed the killing, but says he was then ignorant, thus denying that the act made him a disbeliever.
rows.anchor: أي فعلت تلك الفعلة يريد قتل القبطي

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: He also interprets الضالين as ‘ignorant’.
rows.anchor: وكذا قال مجاهد { من الضالين } من الجاهلين

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: He explains the ignorance as not knowing that the blow would kill.
rows.anchor: ابن زيد: من الجاهلين بأن الوكزة تبلغ القتل

rows.speaker: مصحف عبد الله
rows.claim: The codex of Abdullah reads من الجاهلين (‘among the ignorant’) in place of من الضالين.
rows.anchor: وفي مصحف عبد الله { من الجاهلين }

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: He interprets الضالين as forgetful.
rows.anchor: وقيل: { وأنا من الضالين } من الناسين قاله أبو عبيدة

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another interpretation is that Moses was still outside prophethood and had received no divine instruction about the act, so he was not blameworthy then.
rows.anchor: وقيل: { وأنا من الضالين } عن النبوة ولم يأتني عن الله فيه شيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh’s upbringing of Moses does not conflict with prophethood or forbearance; accidental killing, or killing before a revealed law, does not invalidate prophethood.
rows.anchor: وبين بهذا أن التربية فيهم لا تنافي النبوة والحلم على الناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses fled to Midian when he feared Pharaoh’s people after the killing, as also related in 28:21.
rows.anchor: أي خرجت من بينكم إلى مدين كما في سورة «القصص»

rows.speaker: السدي وغيره
rows.claim: They interpret the حكم God gave Moses as prophethood.
rows.anchor: يعني النبوة عن السدي وغيره

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: He interprets it as teaching the Torah, which contains God’s law.
rows.anchor: الزجاج: تعليم التوراة التي فيها حكم الله

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another interpretation is that حكم means knowledge and understanding.
rows.anchor: وقيل علما وفهما

rows.speaker: السدي والطبري والفراء
rows.claim: They read Moses as acknowledging the upbringing as a favor, while adding that Pharaoh’s enslavement of others does not negate Moses’ message.
rows.anchor: هذا الكلام من موسى عليه السلام على جهة الإقرار بالنعمة

rows.speaker: قتادة وغيره
rows.claim: They take Moses to deny the alleged favor: Pharaoh enslaved and killed his people, so raising Moses was no favor he should claim.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هو من موسى عليه السلام على جهة الإنكار

rows.speaker: الأخفش والفراء
rows.claim: They supply an omitted interrogative alif, reading ‘Is that a favor?’; al-Nahhas and others reject deleting the alif unless أم occurs.
rows.anchor: وقيل: فيه تقدير استفهام أي أو تلك نعمة؟

rows.speaker: النحاس
rows.claim: He says deleting the interrogative alif is impossible because it changes the meaning, except where أم appears, as in poetry.
rows.anchor: قال النحاس: وهذا لا يجوز لأن ألف الاستفهام تحدث معنى

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: He allows omission of the interrogative alif in verbs of doubt, citing ترى زيدا منطلقا for أترى; Ali ibn Sulayman says this came from common speech.
rows.anchor: قاله الفراء. قال: يجوز حذف ألف الاستفهام في أفعال الشك

rows.speaker: الثعلبي
rows.claim: He transmits al-Farra’s analogy to Abraham’s rhetorical ‘This is my lord’ and ‘Are they the immortals?’ and poetry where the interrogative alif is omitted.
rows.anchor: الثعلبي: قال الفراء ومن قال إنها إنكار

rows.speaker: الغزنوي
rows.claim: He cites a second poem as evidence that the interrogative alif can be omitted without an explicit أم.
rows.anchor: أنشد الغزنوي شاهدا على ترك الألف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He says this poem does show deletion of the interrogative alif without أم, contrary to al-Nahhas’s claim.
rows.anchor: قلت: ففي هذا حذف ألف الاستفهام مع عدم أم خلاف قول النحاس

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: He reads the speech as a rebuke, with or without an explicit question: had Pharaoh not killed Israelite boys, Moses’ parents would have raised him, so Pharaoh should not claim credit.
rows.anchor: وقال الضحاك: إن الكلام خرج مخرج التبكيت والتبكيت يكون باستفهام وبغير استفهام

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another explanation is that Pharaoh cannot boast of raising Moses while humiliating Moses’ people, since a person whose people are humiliated is himself diminished.
rows.anchor: وقيل: معناه كيف تمن بالتربية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: أن عبدت may be nominative as an appositive to نعمة, or accusative with the sense ‘because you enslaved the Children of Israel’; al-Farra says عبدته and أعبدته are synonymous and cites poetry.
rows.anchor: في موضع رفع على البدل من

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After failing to answer Moses’ point about upbringing, Pharaoh challenges the title ‘Lord of the worlds’ by asking what kind of thing the Lord is.
rows.anchor: لما غلب موسى فرعون بالحجة ولم يجد اللعين من تقريره على التربية وغير ذلك حجة رجع إلى معارضة موسى

rows.speaker: مكي وغيره
rows.claim: They say Pharaoh asks ما as one asks about a genus; elsewhere he asks من, perhaps in a different setting. God has no genus because genera are created.
rows.anchor: قال مكي وغيره: كما يستفهم عن الأجناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses answers with attributes evident from creation, which no creature shares; recognizing Pharaoh’s ignorance, he points to God’s immense power instead of a genus.
rows.anchor: فأتى موسى بالصفات الدالة على الله من مخلوقاته التي لا يشاركه فيها مخلوق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh’s ‘Will you not listen?’ is an incitement and expression of amazement at what he calls foolishness, since the people believed Pharaoh and his predecessors were gods.
rows.anchor: على معنى الإغراء والتعجب من سفه المقالة إذ كانت عقيدة القوم أن فرعون ربهم ومعبودهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: By naming their earliest ancestors, Moses invokes people they know have died: they came into being after nonexistence and must have a maker.
rows.anchor: لأنهم يعلمون أنه قد كان لهم آباء وأنهم قد فنوا وأنه لا بد لهم من مغير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh mocks Moses as mad because he is not answering Pharaoh’s question in the way he expects.
rows.anchor: فقال فرعون حينئذ على جهة الاستخفاف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses contrasts God’s dominion over east and west with Pharaoh’s limited rule over one land, where he cannot control everyone or kill whom he wishes.
rows.anchor: أن ليس ملكه كملكك لأنك إنما تملك بلدا واحدا لا يجوز أمرك في غيره

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view is that Moses understood Pharaoh genuinely wanted to know the one he asked about, so he gave the proper route to knowing the Lord.
rows.anchor: وقيل: علم موسى عليه السلام أن قصده في السؤال معرفة من سأل عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Once cornered by the argument, Pharaoh returns to coercion and threatens prison; he avoids asking for proof because that would concede another god.
rows.anchor: ثم لما انقطع فرعون لعنه الله في باب الحجة رجع إلى الاستعلاء والتغلب فتوعد موسى بالسجن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says Pharaoh was so terrified that he could not control his urine; his prison was feared because prisoners died there and were never released.
rows.anchor: وكان فيما يروى أنه يفزع منه فزعا شديدا حتى كان اللعين لا يمسك بوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses gently addresses Pharaoh in hope of belief, asking whether he would listen if Moses brought a clear sign.
rows.anchor: له على جهة اللطف به والطمع في إيمانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh hopes to find an opening to challenge the sign and demands that Moses produce it if he is truthful.
rows.anchor: فلما سمع فرعون ذلك طمع في أن يجد أثناءه موضع معارضة

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: The conditional phrase needs no separate answer because the preceding words already supply it.
rows.anchor: ولم يحتج الشرط إلى جواب عند سيبويه لأن ما تقدم يكفي منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses throws his staff from his hand, and what God had announced about its story takes place.
rows.anchor: { فألقى موسى عصاه } من يده فكان ما أخبر الله من قصته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The story of Abraham confronts the idolaters’ profound ignorance: they reject the faith of their own forefather; the account binds them by argument and exposes his criticism of their worship.
rows.anchor: نبه المشركين على فرط جهلهم إذ رغبوا عن اعتقاد إبراهيم ودينه وهو أبوهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority lighten the second hamza in نبأ إبراهيم, which he considers best because readers likewise agree to lighten the second hamza in a single word such as آدم.
rows.anchor: والجمهور من القراء على تخفيف الهمزة الثانية وهو أحسن الوجوه لأنهم قد أجمعوا على تخفيف الثانية من كلمة واحدة نحو آدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other possible pronunciations are to pronounce both hamzas, lighten both, or lighten the first; a fifth option assimilates one hamza into the other but is linguistically remote.
rows.anchor: وإن شئت حققتهما فقلت: { نبأ إبراهيم }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Assimilating the hamzas is remote because it combines two hamzas as if in one word, although assimilation is natural in the pattern فعّال.
rows.anchor: وثم وجه خامس إلا أنه بعيد في العربية وهو أن يدغم الهمزة في الهمزة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses’ question ما تعبدون means ‘What do you worship?’
rows.anchor: أي أي شيء تعبدون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their idols were made from gold, silver, copper, iron, and wood.
rows.anchor: وكانت أصنامهم من ذهب وفضة ونحاس وحديد وخشب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: فنظل لها عاكفين means they persist in worshipping the idols; it describes their ongoing condition, not a particular time.
rows.anchor: أي فنقيم على عبادتها. وليس المراد وقتا معينا

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view is that they worshipped idols by day and planets by night; ظل is used for daytime and بات for nighttime activity.
rows.anchor: وقيل: كانوا يعبدونها بالنهار دون الليل، وكانوا في الليل يعبدون الكواكب

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: He says هل يسمعونكم contains an ellipsis: it means ‘do they hear from you?’ or ‘do they hear your prayers?’; a line of poetry similarly omits a complement, and الأبق is glossed as flax (or hemp in al-Sihah).
rows.anchor: قال الأخفش: فيه حذف والمعنى:

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: He reports a reading with damma on the ya, asking whether the idols make their worshippers hear their sounds.
rows.anchor: وروي عن قتادة أنه قرأ { هل يسمعونكم } بضم الياء أي هل يسمعونكم أصواتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham asks whether the idols benefit or harm them, grant provision, or control good and evil; if they do neither, worship makes no sense.
rows.anchor: أي هل تنفعكم هذه الأصنام وترزقكم، أو تملك لكم خيرا أو ضرا إن عصيتم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people abandon argument and appeal to ancestral imitation without proof.
rows.anchor: فنزعوا إلى التقليد من غير حجة ولا دليل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: الأقدمون means the earlier, first ancestors.
rows.anchor: { أنتم وآباؤكم الأقدمون } الأولون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: عدو is a singular form used for a group and can also be used of a woman; al-Farra permits both عدو الله and عدوة الله, while Ali ibn Sulayman explains the feminine forms differently.
rows.anchor: { فإنهم عدو لي } واحد يؤدي عن جماعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The idols are called Abraham’s enemies because, if worshipped, they will oppose their worshippers on Judgment Day, as stated at 19:82.
rows.anchor: ووصف الجماد بالعداوة بمعنى أنهم عدو لي إن عبدتهم يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: He takes the wording as inverted: its sense is ‘I am their enemy,’ since one whom you oppose becomes your enemy.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء: هو من المقلوب مجازه فإني عدو لهم لأن من عاديته عاداك

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: He interprets except the Lord of the worlds as ‘except the worshipper of the Lord of the worlds,’ with the noun عابد omitted.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي: أي إلا من عبد رب العالمين

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق الزجاج
rows.claim: Grammarians take the exception as disconnected; al-Zajjaj also allows a connected exception if Abraham’s people worshipped God alongside idols, so he disavows their objects except God.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق الزجاج: قال النحويون هو استثناء ليس من الأول

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: He applies the exception only to the idols: if Abraham worshipped them, they would be his enemies on Judgment Day.
rows.anchor: وتأوله الفراء على الأصنام وحدها والمعنى عنده: فإنهم لو عبدتهم عدو لي يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: الجرجاني
rows.claim: He estimates the phrase as excluding the Lord of the worlds from the objects worshipped by Abraham’s people, then saying the idols are his enemies; وإلا here means ‘besides’ or ‘other than,’ as in 44:56.
rows.anchor: وقال الجرجاني: تقديره: أفرأيتم ما كنتم تعبدون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exception particle can mean دون or سوى (‘other than’), illustrated by 44:56, where the phrase means they will taste no death besides the first death.
rows.anchor: وإلا بمعنى دون وسوى كقوله:
